query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace carbon content (~0.1 at.%) into the titanium‐ and nickel‐dominated single‐phase FCC high-entropy alloy and applying a tailored heat-treatment to induce in-situ precipitation of nano-scale TiC will significantly improve its high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the alloy produced without carbon.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are primary constituents (without controlled secondary phase formation).
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled microalloying level of carbon (~0.1 at.%) during synthesis, then perform a post-synthesis heat-treatment designed to nucleate and disperse nano-scale TiC precipitates uniformly within the matrix and along grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and creep) conducted in the temperature range of approximately 700–1000 °C, in inert or low-oxidation environments; applicable to compositions where Ti and Ni dominate the primary solid-solution state.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed TiC precipitates distributed throughout the FCC matrix and along critical grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale TiC particles are expected to act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion and inhibit grain-boundary sliding, thereby producing dual benefits of dispersion strengthening and grain refinement. This hinders the mobility of thermally activated dislocations at high temperature and improves creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-added alloy is predicted to show an improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength (on the order of 15–20% higher) and extended creep life compared to the carbon-free baseline, while maintaining acceptable ductility.
generation.baseline: The same Ti–Ni dominated single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy produced without any controlled carbon addition (and therefore without in-situ TiC formation).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloys that are processed to maintain a single-phase FCC structure. Testing is valid under high-temperature ranges (700–1000 °C) in environments that minimize oxidation, and the results are only applicable as long as the precipitates remain nano-scale and do not coarsen into deleterious networks.
generation.uncertainty: While dispersion strengthening via nanoparticles has been effective in other alloy systems (e.g., as shown in studies on nanoparticle‐modified superalloys, PMC10222657 and effects of Ti on strengthening in PMC7040714), it is uncertain how well controlled in-situ TiC precipitation will be achieved in a Ti–Ni dominant HEA given Ti’s strong carbide-forming tendency. Moreover, the potential trade-off between increased strength and reduced ductility, as highlighted by conflicting outcomes in traditional high-Ti HEAs (PMC11123020), remains to be clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Ti–Ni based high-entropy alloy using identical processing routes. One batch is produced with a trace carbon addition (~0.1 at.%), followed by a heat-treatment schedule optimized for nucleating nano-scale TiC precipitates, while the control batch is produced without carbon. Conduct elevated-temperature tensile tests and creep tests at temperatures such as 700 °C, 850 °C, and 1000 °C.
measurements: Elevated-temperature yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Microstructural analyses by TEM/SEM to assess the presence, size, and distribution of TiC precipitates
Grain size and phase distribution evaluations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added alloy does not achieve a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than ~15% gain) in yield strength or creep resistance compared to the baseline, or if the microstructural analyses reveal coarse or continuous carbide formations leading to embrittlement, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
